steps.title: Check current kmesh deployment
steps.description:
Verify your kmesh version and configuration:
```bash
kubectl get pods -n kmesh -l app.kubernetes.io/name=kmesh
helm list -n kmesh 2>/dev/null || echo "Not installed via Helm"
```
This feature requires a working kmesh installation.

steps.title: Review kmesh configuration
steps.description:
Inspect the relevant kmesh configuration:
```bash
kubectl get all -n kmesh -l app.kubernetes.io/name=kmesh
kubectl get configmap -n kmesh -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=kmesh
```
### **Description:**

  Build a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes Kmesh's capabilities as callable tools for AI agents (Claude, Cursor, GitHub Copilot).

resolution.summary:
Correction to my last comment, and an update.

I stood up a kind cluster with Istio and a real kmesh-daemon to test the prototype against something other than my stub, and the first thing it did was catch a mistake of mine.

I said the daemon registers `cni installer` as a logger. It doesn't.
codeSnippets:
So the value is smaller than I first described. It doesn't rescue a listed-but-unqueryable logger, it turns a bare transport 400 into the daemon's own message. Still worth having, since `subsys=cni installer` and `subsys=cache/v2` show up in every log line and look like logger names, but I oversold it and wanted to say so.

The rest held up. Against the real daemon the mode probe behaves exactly as assumed, `/debug/config_dump/bpf/dual-engine` answers 200 and `kernel-native` answers 400, so mode detection resolved `dual-engine` on its own with no input. All six tools ran against it, and `get_bpf_maps` came back with real map contents including the actual backend IP.
